title: Build a server and a client that talk
objective: By the end of this lesson you have a working TCP server and client in C that exchange a length-prefixed message correctly, including messages too large to arrive in one read.

blocks.text: Everything in this module comes together here. The program is small, and almost all of its correctness lives in two helper functions and one design decision — how a receiver knows where a message ends.
The protocol: four bytes, then that many

blocks.caption: A length prefix, which is the simplest thing that works
lines: [ 4-byte length, network byte order ][ that many bytes of message ]
/* The receiver reads exactly 4 bytes, converts them, then reads exactly
that many. No guessing, no scanning for a delimiter, and it works for
binary data — which a delimiter-based protocol does not, without escaping. */

blocks.text: The two functions that make it correct

blocks.caption: read_all and write_all
lines: /* The two functions every network program needs, and most first attempts omit. */
static int read_all(int fd, void *buf, size_t n) {
ssize_t r = read(fd, (char *)buf + got, n - got);
got += (size_t)r;                           /* a short read is normal */
static int write_all(int fd, const void *buf, size_t n) {
ssize_t w = write(fd, (const char *)buf + sent, n - sent);
sent += (size_t)w;                          /* a partial write is normal */

blocks.title: These two loops are the whole lesson
blocks.text: Every point made earlier in this module is in them: a short read is normal, a partial write is normal, EINTR means retry rather than fail, and read returning 0 means the peer closed. A network program without these loops works perfectly on a local connection and fails in production, which is exactly the class of bug worth eliminating by construction rather than by testing.

blocks.caption: Complete, with the error handling that is not optional
lines: addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_LOOPBACK);   /* this machine only, while testing */
if (bind(listener, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof addr) < 0) { perror("bind"); return 1; }
struct sockaddr_in peer; socklen_t plen = sizeof peer;
if (conn < 0) { perror("accept"); continue; }   /* one failure must not end the server */
if (len > MAX_MESSAGE) { close(conn); continue; }   /* never trust a length off the wire */
if (read_all(conn, body, len) != 1) { free(body); close(conn); continue; }

blocks.title: Three lines that are easy to leave out, and each one is a real defect
blocks.text: Not closing the connection leaves it in CLOSE_WAIT until descriptors run out, exactly as the previous lesson showed. Not checking the length before allocating lets a client send a four-byte header claiming four gigabytes. Ending the loop when accept() fails turns one transient error into an outage. All three look like tidying up; all three are the difference between a demonstration and a program.

blocks.caption: Send, then read the reply back
lines: if (connect(fd, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof addr) < 0) { perror("connect"); return 1; }
if (read_all(fd, &back_net, sizeof back_net) != 1) { /* no reply */ return 1; }
if (back > MAX_MSG) { /* the same rule the server follows: never trust a length off the wire */ return 1; }
if (!buf) { /* malloc can fail, and back came from the network */ return 1; }
if (read_all(fd, buf, back) != 1) { /* short reply */ return 1; }
printf("echoed %u bytes, match=%s\n", back, strcmp(buf, msg) == 0 ? "yes" : "no");

blocks.text: Proving it — and why the obvious test does not
The obvious test is to send a large message and see whether it arrives intact. That test is not good enough, and finding out why is the most useful thing in this lesson.

blocks.caption: Measured: the broken version passing every size on loopback
lines: # A server using a single read() instead of the loop, tested over 127.0.0.1:
# The loopback interface on that machine had an MTU of 16384 and buffers
# large enough that every message arrived in one piece. The bug was there
# the whole time and no size revealed it.

blocks.title: This is why the bug reaches production
blocks.text: Testing on loopback cannot show it. The message is handed over in memory, arrives complete, and one read() gets all of it — at every size tried, up to 64,000 bytes. Across a real network the same message is split by the path's MTU and delayed by congestion, and the single read returns only part. A test that passes locally and fails in production is the defining property of this defect, so the test has to reproduce the condition rather than the size.

Make the sender slow instead of making the message large. A client that sends the header, pauses, sends half the body, pauses, and sends the rest reproduces exactly what a real network does — and it does so deterministically, on loopback, in two seconds.

blocks.caption: Measured with a sender that pauses mid-message
lines: /* client: write the header, sleep(2), write half the body, sleep(2), write the rest */
header said 2000 bytes; the body actually held 1000 characters
header said 2000 bytes; the body held 2000 characters
/* Same programs, same 2000-byte message, same machine. The only difference
is whether the receiver loops until it has what the header promised. */

blocks.title: Build it, then break it in the ways that matter
steps: Write both programs as above and confirm a short message round-trips
Replace read_all with a single read() and test at 2,000, then 20,000, then 64,000 bytes
Note that it passes every time on loopback — the bug is present and invisible
Now write a second client that sends the header, sleeps two seconds, sends half the body, sleeps again, and sends the rest
Run that client against the single-read server and confirm match=NO
Have the server print how many characters the body actually held and confirm it is half
Put read_all back and confirm the same slow client now succeeds
Then break it three more ways: remove close(conn) and find CLOSE_WAIT; remove the length check and send a header claiming 4000000000; make a failed accept() end the loop
blocks.expected: A broken server that passes every size test on loopback, and the same server failing immediately against a sender that pauses mid-message. That contrast is the lesson: the defect is not about size, it is about whether the data arrives in one piece — so the test must control arrival, not volume. The three deliberate defects after that are ones you will now recognise in someone else's code on sight.

cheatsheet: Length prefix: 4 bytes in network byte order, then exactly that many
read_all loops until it has n bytes; write_all loops until it has sent n
EINTR means retry, read returning 0 means the peer closed, both need handling
Test by controlling ARRIVAL, not volume: make the sender pause mid-message. A large message proves nothing on its own — it arrived in one piece here at every size up to 64,000 bytes
close() every accepted connection or CLOSE_WAIT accumulates
Never allocate based on a length from the network without checking it first
A failed accept() must continue the loop, not end the server
SO_REUSEADDR before bind; INADDR_LOOPBACK while testing
Verified: this program echoed 21, 16 and 5000 bytes with exact matches

checkpoint.prompt: You replace read_all with a single read() and test messages up to 64,000 bytes over loopback. Everything passes. What have you established?

choices.C: That the server is fast enough
choices.D: That 64,000 bytes is under the limit

checkpoint.explanation: A single read gets all of it; the defect only appears when data arrives split. Measured: the single-read version passed at 2,000, 5,000, 20,000, 30,000, 50,000 and 64,000 bytes on loopback. It failed immediately against a sender that paused mid-message, receiving 1000 characters of a 2000-byte body. Test the condition, not the size.

checkpoint.prompt: Why must the server check the length before calling malloc?

choices.A: The length must be a multiple of four
choices.B: malloc becomes slow for very large allocation sizes
choices.C: The length comes from an untrusted client

checkpoint.explanation: Four bytes from an untrusted source should never size an allocation unchecked. This is the C course's rule about hostile input, in its network form. A client can claim any value it likes, including one chosen to exhaust memory.

checkpoint.prompt: Your server stops accepting connections after running for a while, and ss shows many CLOSE_WAIT entries. What did you forget?

choices.A: A listen() backlog value set too small for the load

checkpoint.explanation: Each unclosed connection holds a descriptor. When the process reaches its limit, accept() fails and no new client can be served — with the cause visible in the state listing.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a length prefix handle binary data better than a delimiter?

choices.A: A delimiter byte can also occur inside the data
choices.B: It uses fewer bytes on the wire for small messages
choices.C: Delimiters are not allowed in TCP

checkpoint.explanation: Binary content needs escaping; a length does not. With a length, the receiver knows exactly how many bytes to read and their content is irrelevant. With a delimiter, any occurrence inside the payload must be escaped, and forgetting to is a classic parsing bug.

checkpoint.prompt: What does TCP preserve for an application?

choices.A: Each send call becomes one matching recv call
choices.B: The ends of packets and message types
choices.D: An ordered byte stream without built-in message ends

checkpoint.explanation: A receiver must frame its own messages because read calls do not preserve protocol message ends.

checkpoint.prompt: What must a length-prefixed receiver do before allocation?

choices.A: Validate the announced length against a limit
choices.B: Allocate whatever size the peer requests
choices.C: Treat the first received bytes as a complete body
choices.D: Use the local CPU word size as the protocol limit

checkpoint.explanation: Network length fields are untrusted input and must be bounded before allocating.

checkpoint.prompt: What does accept return on success?

choices.A: The same listening descriptor with client data ready
choices.B: The received-byte count from the peer
choices.D: The peer's port number as a descriptor

checkpoint.explanation: The listening socket remains available while each accepted connection gets its own descriptor.

checkpoint.prompt: Why loop around send or write on a socket?

choices.A: TCP guarantees each call writes the full buffer
choices.B: A successful call can send only part of the buffer
choices.C: The loop turns separate sends into messages
choices.D: It makes read return a whole request

checkpoint.explanation: The return count tells how much was sent; remaining bytes still need handling.

checkpoint.prompt: What does recv returning zero mean after a positive-length request on a TCP socket?

choices.A: The peer performed an orderly shutdown
choices.B: No data has arrived yet, so retry immediately
choices.D: The peer's address can no longer be queried

checkpoint.explanation: After a positive-length request, zero signals end of the peer byte stream, not another payload byte.

checkpoint.prompt: Why set a maximum message size?

choices.C: To choose the kernel receive buffer
choices.D: To bound memory and work from untrusted peers

checkpoint.explanation: A protocol limit keeps one client from demanding an unbounded allocation.

choices.A: The local application closed before the peer
choices.B: The peer closed and the local process has not closed
choices.C: The TCP handshake is awaiting accept
choices.D: A lost packet must be retransmitted

checkpoint.explanation: The application normally needs to close its descriptor after finishing its response.

checkpoint.prompt: Why encode multi-byte protocol integers explicitly?

choices.A: TCP chooses the byte order for integers
choices.B: One CPU architecture makes values portable
choices.C: Peers may use different native byte orders
choices.D: The first recv converts all data automatically

checkpoint.explanation: Network byte order provides a shared representation across hosts.

checkpoint.prompt: On Linux, what does listen backlog limit?

choices.A: The queue of fully established connections waiting for accept
choices.B: The queue of half-open SYN requests
choices.C: Bytes queued for one accepted socket
choices.D: The number of descriptors a process may open

checkpoint.explanation: On Linux, backlog limits fully established sockets waiting for accept; a full queue can delay or refuse new attempts.

choices.A: To flush unread data onto the network
choices.B: To make the listening socket accept faster
choices.C: To convert the connection into UDP
choices.D: To release its descriptor and connection resources

checkpoint.explanation: Leaving descriptors open eventually reaches process limits and stops new work.

checkpoint.prompt: What should a protocol parser retain across partial reads?

choices.A: Only the most recent recv buffer
choices.B: Its framing state and bytes received so far
choices.D: One operating-system thread for every message

checkpoint.explanation: TCP delivery can split fields and bodies, so parsing continues across calls.
